116.scenario: A company creates an application, publishes new versions, and continually improves the associated service offerings, while a separate partner operates the infrastructure.
116.question_text: Which role does the company mainly perform?
116.explanation: The digital product vendor is responsible for the creation and continual improvement of digital products and their associated service offerings. This role may be distinct from the one that operates the infrastructure or provides certain service components.

A.rationale: The company creates and improves the digital product and its associated offerings: that is the vendor role.

B.rationale: The scenario mainly highlights the responsibility for creating the product, not consuming it.

C.rationale: Relationship management nurtures stakeholder links; the scenario describes creating the product.

D.rationale: The service desk is a point of contact, not a role responsible for product creation.

117.scenario: A telecom operator offers the same standard subscription to thousands of customers, with little personalisation and an identical contract for all.
117.question_text: Which type of service relationship is most likely?
117.explanation: A basic relationship is generally standardised, efficiency-oriented, and characterised by limited personalisation. It suits broadly uniform offerings aimed at many consumers.

A.rationale: The standard offering and the low degree of adaptation characterise a basic relationship.

B.rationale: A cooperative relationship involves more adaptation and joint improvement.

C.rationale: A collaborative relationship rests on a strategic partnership and strong interdependence.

D.rationale: This term is not one of the service relationship types defined in this model.

118.scenario: A managed service provider adapts its processes to a customer's specific requirements, and both parties regularly review operational improvements.
118.question_text: Which type of service relationship is described?
118.explanation: A cooperative relationship includes greater personalisation and regular collaboration aimed at improving services. It goes beyond a standard offering without necessarily reaching the strategic interdependence of a collaborative partnership.

A.rationale: Process adaptation and joint improvement reviews correspond to active cooperation.

B.rationale: A basic relationship is more standardised and focused on transactional efficiency.

C.rationale: The scenario does not mention shared strategy, shared risks, or strong interdependence.

D.rationale: This category is not one of the ITIL service relationship types.

119.scenario: Two organisations jointly design a new platform, share risks, coordinate their roadmaps, and strongly depend on each other to reach a common goal.
119.question_text: Which type of service relationship is most appropriate?
119.explanation: A collaborative relationship is strategic and rests on trust, joint innovation, shared risks, and strong interdependence. The organisations pursue growth or common outcomes together.

A.rationale: Shared strategy, innovation, and interdependence characterise this type of relationship.

B.rationale: Cooperation may include joint improvements but not necessarily such a strong strategic dependency.

C.rationale: A basic relationship favours a standard offering and limited interactions.

D.rationale: This is not an official service relationship type in this classification.

120.question_text: Which statement about the service journey is correct?
120.explanation: The service journey represents the whole set of activities and interactions performed by the provider and the consumer. It is not necessarily linear and may include loops, parallel steps, and different paths.

A.text: It may include loops, parallel steps, and several paths
A.rationale: The service journey is not linear: it can loop and follow several paths.

B.text: It starts when the service level agreement is signed
B.rationale: The journey starts well before, when needs and offerings are explored.

C.text: It is managed by the provider, without consumer involvement
C.rationale: The service journey involves the activities and interactions of all organisations involved.

D.text: It follows one fixed sequence of steps that is the same for each consumer
D.rationale: The journey is not linear: it can include loops and several paths.

121.question_text: Which of the following best defines service quality?
121.explanation: Service quality is the sum of the characteristics of a service that are relevant to satisfying expressed or implied needs. It cannot be reduced to a single technical metric.

A.text: The totality of characteristics that satisfy stated and implied needs
A.rationale: That is the definition of service quality.

B.text: One or more metrics that define expected or achieved service performance
B.rationale: That describes a service level, not service quality.

C.text: The satisfaction reported by the sponsor in the annual review
C.rationale: Quality is not reduced to the opinion of a single role.

D.text: The number of service actions executed by the provider
D.rationale: Activity volume does not demonstrate that the consumer's needs are met.

122.question_text: What is a service level according to ITIL Foundation (Version 5)?
122.explanation: A service level is a set of metrics that defines the expected or actually achieved quality. It makes expectations and results precise enough to be tracked and evaluated.

A.text: A set of metrics defining expected or achieved service quality
A.rationale: A service level translates quality into defined metrics.

B.text: A general statement of the provider's vision
B.rationale: A vision gives direction but does not define measurable quality expectations.

C.text: A list of incidents resolved during the month
C.rationale: That list can feed reports but does not by itself constitute a service level.

D.text: A classification of the relationship as basic, cooperative, or collaborative
D.rationale: Relationship types describe the nature of collaboration, not measured quality.

123.question_text: Which statement correctly describes a service level agreement (SLA)?
123.explanation: An SLA is a documented agreement between a service provider and a customer. It identifies the required services and the expected service levels, generally through relevant metrics.

A.text: A documented agreement between provider and customer on services and expected levels
A.rationale: This option covers the essential parties and content of an SLA.

B.text: An internal document defining the responsibilities and procedures of the technical team
B.rationale: An SLA links the provider and the customer; it is not limited to internal organisation.

C.text: A report presenting the service levels actually achieved over a period
C.rationale: A report measures results, while an SLA formalises the agreed services and expectations.

D.text: A formal description of services designed for a target consumer group
D.rationale: That describes a service offering, not an SLA.

124.scenario: A tender requires low-carbon energy, transparent supply chains, and responsible employment practices.
124.question_text: Which service quality concept is mainly involved?
124.explanation: Sustainability ensures that a product or service meets and will continue to meet expectations related to environmental protection, social progress, and economic growth. The requirements described therefore go beyond mere technical performance.

A.rationale: Environmental, social, and economic criteria directly fall under sustainability.

B.rationale: Warranty concerns assurance that a service will meet agreed conditions of use.

C.rationale: Utility describes what the service does and its ability to meet a functional need.

D.rationale: Observability concerns inferring the internal state of a system from its outputs.

125.scenario: A company uses an external cloud service to host its own platform, then provides that platform as a service to its customers.
125.question_text: Which statement is the most correct?
125.explanation: The same organisation can take on different roles in several service relationships. It is a consumer with respect to the cloud provider and a provider with respect to the users of its platform.

A.text: It consumes the cloud service and provides its platform, in two relationships
A.rationale: An organisation can be a consumer in one relationship and a provider in another.

B.text: It is a provider in both relationships because it bills its customers
B.rationale: Towards the cloud provider, the company is a consumer.

C.text: It is a consumer in both relationships because it relies on external infrastructure
C.rationale: Towards its customers, the company is a provider.

D.text: It acts as the sponsor of the cloud provider in both relationships
D.rationale: The sponsor authorises budget on the consumer side; it does not describe both relationships.

126.question_text: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between PESTLE factors and the four ITIL dimensions?
126.explanation: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, and Environmental factors are external influences. They can affect each of the four dimensions but do not constitute an additional dimension.

A.text: They influence the four dimensions without forming a fifth dimension
A.rationale: PESTLE helps examine the external environment that acts on all the dimensions.

B.text: They are part of the partners and suppliers dimension
B.rationale: PESTLE factors are external and belong to no dimension.

C.text: They mainly influence the information and technology dimension
C.rationale: PESTLE factors can influence the four dimensions.

D.text: They are internal factors that the organisation controls through the four dimensions
D.rationale: PESTLE factors are external; it is the dimensions that are internal.

127.scenario: An organisation finds that its punitive culture prevents teams from reporting mistakes and sharing feedback.
127.question_text: How should this factor be classified?
127.explanation: Organisational culture is an internal factor mainly belonging to organisations and people. It can strongly influence behaviours, collaboration, and improvement.

A.rationale: Culture is created and maintained within the organisation.

B.rationale: No government decision or external political dynamic is described.

C.rationale: The scenario is not about the natural environment or ecological sustainability.

D.rationale: The issue concerns behaviours and culture, not a technological development.

128.scenario: Strong inflation suddenly raises the costs of licences, energy, and subcontracting contracts.
128.question_text: Which PESTLE factor is mainly illustrated?
128.explanation: Inflation, interest rates, costs, and market conditions are economic factors. They can change sourcing decisions, budgets, and the viability of offerings.

A.rationale: Inflation is an economic development directly affecting costs.

B.rationale: Social factors mainly concern behaviours, expectations, and demographic changes.

C.rationale: No new legal obligation is at the origin of the described increase.

D.rationale: The technologies concerned cost more, but the triggering factor is economic.

129.scenario: The organization commits to reducing the carbon footprint of its data centres and the energy consumption of its services.
129.question_text: Which PESTLE factor is most directly concerned by this commitment?
129.explanation: Reducing carbon footprint and energy consumption falls under the environmental PESTLE factor.

A.rationale: The main objective concerns the impact on the natural environment.

B.rationale: The form of the requirement is regulatory, but its direct object is emissions reduction.

C.rationale: Technology can help, but the emissions reduction objective is environmental.

D.rationale: Costs may result from it, but they are not the objective described.

130.question_text: Which scope belongs to the "information and technology" dimension?
130.explanation: This dimension covers the information, knowledge, and technologies used both in products and services and in the organisation's management system. It is therefore not limited to user-visible tools or to internal data only.

A.text: The information, knowledge, and technologies used in products and services
A.rationale: That is the scope of the information and technology dimension.

B.text: The roles, skills, and culture needed to manage products and services
B.rationale: That belongs to the organizations and people dimension.

C.text: The workflows and activities that create value for consumers
C.rationale: That belongs to the value streams and processes dimension.

D.text: The external organisations involved in delivering, supporting, and improving services
D.rationale: That belongs to the partners and suppliers dimension.

131.topic: Introduction to the ITIL product and service lifecycle
131.question_text: Which statement best describes the eight ITIL product and service lifecycle activities?
131.explanation: The activities discover, design, acquire, build, transition, operate, deliver, and support are interconnected. They can be repeated, overlap, and be used in different orders depending on the context.

A.text: They are used iteratively and not necessarily sequentially
A.rationale: The ITIL lifecycle is flexible and allows for loops and parallel activities.

B.text: They are completed once, in order from Discover to Support
B.rationale: The activities are iterative and non-sequential; the listed order is not mandatory.

C.text: Build and Transition are the activities that can be repeated
C.rationale: Any activity can be repeated and lead to any other.

D.text: Each activity is assigned to a different organisation
D.rationale: The activities do not map to separate organisations.

132.scenario: A team compares suppliers, negotiates terms, and allocates cloud resources to enable the extension of a service.
132.question_text: Which lifecycle activity is mainly being performed?
132.explanation: The "acquire" activity aims to obtain, secure, and effectively allocate the necessary resources. It also takes into account their availability, sustainability, and ability to scale.

A.rationale: Selecting suppliers and allocating resources are directly part of acquisition.

B.rationale: Building mainly consists of developing, integrating, and testing the solution's components.

C.rationale: Transition prepares and moves changes into the environments where they will be used.

D.rationale: Operate concerns the ongoing running and monitoring of products and systems.

133.scenario: Developers integrate components, configure the infrastructure, run tests, and produce the solution's documentation.
133.question_text: Which lifecycle activity is mainly illustrated?
133.explanation: Build turns designs into functional solutions by developing, configuring, integrating, and testing components. The necessary documentation can also be produced during this activity.

A.rationale: The described tasks turn the design into a usable and tested solution.

B.rationale: Acquire obtains the resources but does not mainly cover their technical integration.

C.rationale: Deliver focuses on providing services to users and their routine interactions.

D.rationale: Discover aims to understand needs, opportunities, and constraints before implementation.

134.scenario: A team activates accounts for new users, handles routine SLA-covered requests, and collects feedback after use.
134.question_text: Which lifecycle activity is mainly involved?
134.explanation: Deliver aims to provide services to users, notably through onboarding and offboarding users, handling normal interactions, and collecting feedback. It differs from support, which is mainly reactive to incidents.

A.rationale: User onboarding and routine service provision sit at the heart of this activity.

B.rationale: Operate maintains and monitors the underlying products and systems.

C.rationale: Support mainly handles interruptions, difficulties, and assistance needs.

D.rationale: Design defines the solution and expected experience before delivery.

135.scenario: After a major outage, several teams restore the service, execute disaster recovery, and write a post-incident report.
135.question_text: Which lifecycle activity is mainly illustrated?
135.explanation: Support aims to identify and resolve incidents, restore services, and execute the necessary recovery activities. It also collects information that enables learning after interruptions.

A.rationale: Restoration, disaster recovery, and post-incident analysis fall under support.

B.rationale: Deliver mainly concerns routine provision of the service, not the response to a major outage.

C.rationale: Transition manages the movement of products or changes into their usage environment.

D.rationale: No selection or allocation of new resources is central to the scenario.

136.scenario: Two digital products follow different combinations of value chain activities: one favours frequent releases, the other requires long regulatory validations.
136.question_text: Why can both combinations be ITIL-compliant?
136.explanation: Value chain activities can be combined according to different models to fit the context, the product and service architecture, the objective, and the operating model. ITIL does not prescribe a single sequence.

A.text: Because activities can be combined into patterns tailored to the context and operating model
A.rationale: The value chain allows different combinations depending on how the organisation creates value.

B.text: Because each product can permanently drop the activities that slow its delivery
B.rationale: Adapting a model does not mean ignoring the activities needed for value, control, or quality.

C.text: Because regulated products follow a separate compliance value chain
C.rationale: There is no separate value chain for compliance: it is the value streams that vary with the context.

D.text: Because each management practice imposes its own independent value chain
D.rationale: Practices contribute to activities and value streams; they do not each create a separate chain.

137.scenario: A dashboard indicates that a process is working correctly, but observing daily work reveals manual workarounds and unrecorded delays.
137.question_text: Which action best applies the "start where you are" principle?
137.explanation: This principle recommends assessing the current state objectively. Measures are useful, but they must be complemented by direct observation to avoid an incomplete or misleading picture of what exists.

A.text: Combine dashboard data with direct observation of the work
A.rationale: This approach assesses what exists based on both quantitative evidence and what actually happens.

B.text: Rely on the dashboard because its measures are objective
B.rationale: A measure can omit workarounds or effects that are not recorded; direct observation is still needed.

C.text: Ignore what exists and immediately redesign the process
C.rationale: The clean-slate approach specifically contradicts the assessment of the current state recommended by this principle.

D.text: Automate the manual steps before understanding their cause
D.rationale: Automating without evaluation risks reinforcing an inefficient way of working.

138.question_text: Why does ITIL describe governance as enabling in nature?
138.explanation: Governance sets direction, exercises oversight, and defines the boundaries within which the organisation can act. It must let teams make responsible decisions rather than centralise every operational action.

A.text: It sets direction and control while letting teams act within clear boundaries
A.rationale: Enabling governance combines appropriate control with framed autonomy.

B.text: It performs the lifecycle activities on behalf of the management teams
B.rationale: Governance directs and controls; management teams perform the lifecycle activities.

C.text: It centralises day-to-day operational decisions at the level of the governing body
C.rationale: Centralising daily decisions is the opposite of enabling governance; the governing body does not run day-to-day operations.

D.text: It replaces management by monitoring each team's daily work in detail
D.rationale: Governance monitoring covers performance and compliance, not detailed control of daily work.

139.scenario: A team has a detailed description of the requirements for a future service and an interactive mock-up used to gather feedback.
139.question_text: Which terms best correspond to these two items?
139.explanation: A product specification describes the expected requirements, characteristics, and constraints. A prototype is a preliminary representation used to explore, test, or validate ideas before full implementation.

A.rationale: The formal description of requirements is a specification and the exploratory mock-up is a prototype.

B.rationale: An SLA documents expected service levels and a release is made available for use; neither describes the two items.

C.text: Service offering and value stream map
C.rationale: An offering describes services proposed to consumers and a map represents the flow of work, not requirements or a mock-up.

D.rationale: These terms distinguish a desired effect from a produced deliverable, not the two design artefacts described.

140.scenario: A monitoring tool reports that CPU usage exceeds a threshold, but users have not yet noticed any interruption.
140.question_text: How should this item be classified as a priority?
140.explanation: An event is a significant state change for the management of a service or configuration item. It becomes an incident only if it causes or represents an unplanned interruption or a reduction in quality requiring restoration.

A.rationale: The exceeded threshold is a significant state change with no observed interruption.

B.rationale: No service interruption or degradation is observed yet.

C.rationale: No analysed cause or documented workaround is mentioned.

D.rationale: The signal is generated by monitoring and is not a predefined user request.

141.question_text: Which statement best describes a release?
141.explanation: A release is a set of new or changed configuration items made available for use. It does not necessarily correspond to every individual modification, nor to an automatic deployment.

A.text: A set of new or changed configuration items made available for use
A.rationale: This phrasing matches the ITIL definition of a release.

B.text: A code change recorded in the repository
B.rationale: A recorded change is not necessarily grouped or made available in a release.

C.text: The automatic transfer of validated changes into production
C.rationale: This phrasing rather describes continuous deployment.

D.text: An agreement on a service's quality levels
D.rationale: That notion belongs to SLAs and not to release management.

142.question_text: What is the main role of a test in the product and service lifecycle?
142.explanation: A test evaluates a product, service, or component against predefined criteria. It produces information used to assess its quality, compliance, or fitness for use.

A.text: Evaluate an item against defined criteria to produce information on its quality
A.rationale: A test provides evidence to support a decision, without proving the absence of defects.

B.text: Demonstrate that the product is free of defects before release
B.rationale: Tests reduce uncertainty but generally cannot prove the absence of defects.

C.text: Monitor the live service to detect events and anomalies in production
C.rationale: This describes monitoring and event management in the operate activity, not the role of a test.

D.text: Authorise the deployment of a change after assessing its risks and business impact
D.rationale: Assessing risks and authorising changes belongs to change enablement; tests can inform it.

143.scenario: With every change, developers frequently merge their code into a shared repository and automated tests quickly detect conflicts.
143.explanation: Continuous integration consists of frequently integrating changes into a common code base and verifying them automatically. Its objective is to quickly detect integration defects.

A.rationale: Frequent merges and automated checks are the central characteristics of this practice.

B.rationale: Continuous delivery aims to keep changes in a deployable state, beyond mere integration.

C.rationale: Continuous deployment automatically pushes validated changes into production.

D.rationale: Observability concerns understanding the internal state of a running system.

144.scenario: An organisation automates the build and the tests so that any validated update can be deployed to production at any time, but a manager decides case by case when to deploy it.
144.explanation: Continuous delivery keeps changes in a state ready for production release. Deployment remains an explicit decision, unlike continuous deployment where every validated change is automatically put into production.

A.rationale: Changes are always deployable, but their release still requires a decision.

B.rationale: In continuous deployment, the move to production is automatic after validation.

C.rationale: Continuous integration frequently checks changes without alone guaranteeing they are ready to be delivered.

D.rationale: Release management coordinates what is made available but does not specifically denote this automated capability.

145.scenario: Every change that passes the automated tests is pushed to production without additional authorisation.
145.explanation: Continuous deployment automates the move to production of every change that meets the defined controls. It differs from continuous delivery, where a separate decision to deploy remains.

A.rationale: Automatic release to production after validation is the distinguishing criterion.

B.rationale: Continuous delivery ensures a deployable state but may retain a manual authorisation.

C.rationale: Continuous integration does not require changes to be automatically pushed to production.

D.rationale: The scenario specifically states that no additional authorisation or intervention is required.

146.explanation: Reliability is the ability of a product, service, or configuration item to perform its intended function over a specified period or number of cycles. It differs from availability and recoverability.

A.text: The ability to perform its intended function for a specified period
A.rationale: This answer reflects the definition of reliability: correct operation over a given period.

B.text: The ability to understand a system's internal state from its outputs
B.rationale: This phrasing describes observability rather than reliability.

C.text: The ability to restore normal operation quickly after an interruption
C.rationale: Restoration belongs to recovery and support, not to reliability.

D.text: The proportion of agreed service time during which the service is usable
D.rationale: This describes availability, a related but distinct aspect of warranty.

147.scenario: An organisation makes a team responsible for improving service reliability through measurable objectives, automation, and close collaboration with product teams.
147.explanation: Site Reliability Engineering applies software engineering principles to operations to obtain scalable, reliable services. It relies notably on automation, reliability objectives, and shared responsibility.

A.rationale: The combination of engineering, automation, and reliability objectives matches SRE.

B.rationale: This practice develops relationships with stakeholders and does not define this operational engineering approach.

C.rationale: It handles predefined user requests, not reliability engineering.

D.rationale: Design can incorporate reliability but does not denote the operational approach described.

148.explanation: Observability is the ability to determine or infer the internal state of a system from its outputs, such as logs, metrics, and traces. It does not simply correspond to collecting an isolated indicator.

A.text: The ability to infer the internal state of a system from its outputs
A.rationale: This wording precisely expresses the link between observable outputs and internal state.

B.text: The ability to perform the intended function for a specified period
B.rationale: This definition matches reliability, not observability.

C.text: Collecting a single availability indicator from a monitoring tool
C.rationale: An isolated measure generally does not explain internal state; observability combines metrics, logs, and traces.

D.text: Applying software engineering approaches to infrastructure and operations problems
D.rationale: This phrasing describes Site Reliability Engineering (SRE).

149.scenario: A flood makes the primary site unusable and threatens the continuity of several critical services.
149.question_text: Which ITIL term best describes this situation?
149.explanation: A disaster is a sudden, unplanned event that causes significant damage or losses and requires a coordinated response. It generally exceeds the scope of an ordinary operational incident.

A.rationale: The flood produces major effects requiring recovery and continuity capabilities.

B.rationale: An event is a significant state change, but this term does not convey the destructive scale described.

C.rationale: A service request is a predefined request initiated by a user or their representative.

D.rationale: A known error is an analysed problem whose cause or workaround is documented.

150.scenario: A team has identified that a design defect causes recurring outages. The cause is understood and a workaround is documented, but the defect is not yet fixed.
150.question_text: How should this item be classified?
150.explanation: A known error is a problem that has been analysed but is not yet resolved. Its cause, its workaround, or both are generally documented to help handle the associated incidents.

A.rationale: The cause and workaround are known while the permanent fix remains to be done.

B.rationale: An incident is a specific interruption, whereas the item described is the analysed underlying defect.

C.rationale: An event indicates a state change and does not necessarily represent a known cause.

D.rationale: The defect is not a standard predefined user request.

151.question_text: What is an operating model according to ITIL Foundation (Version 5)?
151.explanation: An operating model represents the way an organisation configures and coordinates its capabilities and resources to fulfil its objective. It links strategy to the concrete organisation of work.

A.text: A representation of how the organisation works to co-create value with stakeholders
A.rationale: The operating model represents how the organisation works to co-create value.

B.text: A preliminary model used to test a product's interface with users
B.rationale: This description matches a product prototype.

C.text: A set of metrics that define the expected or achieved quality of a service
C.rationale: This definition matches a service level.

D.text: A high-level plan describing how the organisation will achieve its long-term objectives
D.rationale: This definition matches a strategy, not the operating model.

152.question_text: What are the two groups of management practices identified in ITIL Foundation (Version 5)?
152.explanation: Version 5 distinguishes general management practices and product and service management practices. This organisation reflects both the organisation's common capabilities and those directly oriented towards its products and services.

A.text: General management practices and product and service management practices
A.rationale: These two headings match the practice groups presented in the syllabus.

B.text: General management, service management, and technical management practices
B.rationale: These are the three ITIL 4 groups; Version 5 removed the technical group.

C.text: Service management practices and technical management practices
C.rationale: These are ITIL 4 groups; Version 5 no longer has a technical group.

D.text: General management practices and technical management practices
D.rationale: The technical group was removed in Version 5; its practices joined the product and service management practices.

153.question_text: Why does the structure of the ITIL practice guides include chapters such as organisations and people, information and technology, partners and suppliers, and value streams and processes?
153.explanation: The guides examine each practice through the four dimensions to avoid a view limited to processes or tools. This structure favours a balanced implementation adapted to context.

A.text: To address each practice in a balanced way across the four dimensions
A.rationale: The structure explicitly links practices to the four-dimensions model.

B.text: To align each practice with the steps of the continual improvement model
B.rationale: The titles cited are the four dimensions, not the steps of the continual improvement model.

C.text: To map each practice to the activities of the value chain
C.rationale: The titles cited correspond to the four dimensions, not to value chain activities.

D.text: To rate each practice against the levels of a maturity model
D.rationale: The titles cited correspond to the dimensions, not to maturity levels.

154.scenario: An organisation wants to improve incident management without inventing its own method from scratch.
154.question_text: What main benefit do the ITIL practice guides bring?
154.explanation: The guides provide consistent, detailed, adaptable recommendations concerning the people, technologies, partners, and value streams of a practice. They speed up adoption of good practice without imposing an identical procedure on every organisation.

A.text: Consistent and adaptable recommendations covering several dimensions of a practice
A.rationale: The guides offer a structured base that must be tailored to the organisation's context.

B.text: A mandatory procedure producing identical results across organisations
B.rationale: ITIL is not prescriptive to the point of imposing identical results regardless of context.

C.text: A complete replacement for the teams' experience
C.rationale: The recommendations complement local knowledge and do not make it useless.

D.text: A list of certified software products to buy
D.rationale: The guides describe capabilities and methods, not a mandatory tool catalogue.

155.question_text: Which statement correctly distinguishes a metric from a critical success factor (CSF)?
155.explanation: A critical success factor describes a condition essential to achieving an objective. A metric is a measure or set of data used to evaluate an aspect of performance or progress.

A.text: A CSF is a necessary precondition for success; a metric measures performance
A.rationale: This distinction separates what must be true to succeed from what is measured.

B.text: A CSF is a numerical target; a metric describes a qualitative condition for success
B.rationale: This reverses the terms: the metric is the measurement, the CSF the precondition.

C.text: A metric defines the strategic objective; a CSF records the performance achieved
C.rationale: Neither term sets the strategy, and a CSF is a precondition, not a record of results.

D.text: A metric and a CSF are two names for the same performance indicator
D.rationale: They are related but play distinct roles in performance management.

156.scenario: Handling a customer order directly produces the paid service, while onboarding a new supplier supports that handling without directly delivering the outcome to the external customer.
156.question_text: How should these two streams be classified?
156.explanation: A core value stream directly delivers value to an external customer. An enabling stream supports one or more core streams by providing the capabilities, resources, or conditions they need.

A.text: The first is core and the second is enabling
A.rationale: The order directly creates customer value, while supplier onboarding supports that creation.

B.text: Both are core because they produce outputs
B.rationale: Producing an output does not mean the stream directly delivers value to an external customer.

C.text: Both are enabling because they use internal resources
C.rationale: Using internal resources does not determine the stream's classification.

D.text: The first is enabling and the second is core
D.rationale: This proposal reverses each stream's direct link to the value delivered to the customer.

157.scenario: A team applies a very detailed procedure to an unprecedented incident involving several suppliers and unpredictable behaviours. The procedure slows the response and hides new information.
157.question_text: Which ITIL approach would be the most appropriate?
157.explanation: Complex thinking recognises that some situations exhibit many interactions, uncertainty, and emergent behaviours. The team should experiment, learn, and adapt its approach rather than assume that a detailed procedure can anticipate everything.

A.text: Use complex thinking and adapt the approach to the level of uncertainty
A.rationale: The unprecedented incident and unpredictable interactions call for an adaptive response.

B.text: Add more mandatory steps to the existing procedure
B.rationale: Additional prescription can make things worse when cause-and-effect relationships are not predictable.

C.text: Let each supplier handle its part independently
C.rationale: Complexity requires more information sharing, not isolation of participants.

D.text: Treat the incident as an enabling value stream without further analysis
D.rationale: Classifying the stream does not resolve the uncertainty or the need to adapt the method.

158.topic: Purpose of value stream mapping and management
158.scenario: An organisation maps its release value stream once, fixes two bottlenecks, and then does not review it again for three years.
158.explanation: Mapping produces a useful representation of the stream's state at a point in time. Value stream management, however, must be ongoing to track changes, measure performance, and identify new improvement opportunities.

A.text: Move from one-off mapping to ongoing value stream management
A.rationale: A value stream evolves with the organisation's products, technologies, teams, and constraints.

B.text: Keep the initial map as the reference model for future releases
B.rationale: An old map may no longer represent how value actually flows.

C.text: Replace the map with a detailed process diagram of each team
C.rationale: A per-team process view loses the end-to-end flow; the need is ongoing value stream management.

D.text: Measure the number of steps removed as the main success indicator
D.rationale: Reducing step count does not by itself demonstrate an improvement in value or performance.

159.scenario: An AI system detects recurring incident trends, forecasts a load increase, and identifies bottlenecks in a value stream.
159.question_text: Which capability from the ITIL AI Capability Model is mainly being used?
159.explanation: Cognition covers analysis, reasoning, pattern detection, and the production of information to support decisions. The system is not merely creating content or communicating: it interprets operational data.

A.rationale: Trend recognition, forecasting, and analysis fall squarely under cognition.

B.rationale: Creation is mainly about generating new content or artefacts.

C.rationale: Communication is about transmitting and adapting information for its audience.

D.rationale: Coordination organises actions and interactions, but is not the central analytical capability in this scenario.

160.scenario: An organisation uses ITIL to continually manage its products and services. It also launches a temporary initiative, with a business case, project governance, and defined deliverables, to replace a platform.
160.question_text: How does PRINCE2 best complement ITIL in this situation?
160.explanation: PRINCE2 provides a structured method to direct and manage a temporary project, while ITIL frames the continual management and improvement of products and services. The two approaches are complementary rather than competing.

A.text: PRINCE2 manages the project; ITIL manages products and services over their lifecycle
A.rationale: Each framework addresses a distinct need and both can be integrated in the same organisation.

B.text: PRINCE2 takes over change enablement and release management for the project's duration
B.rationale: PRINCE2 manages the project; ITIL practices such as change enablement remain in place.

C.text: ITIL manages the project, and PRINCE2 takes over once the platform is live
C.rationale: This reverses the roles: PRINCE2 structures the project and ITIL the ongoing management.

D.text: PRINCE2 defines the value streams used to operate the new platform
D.rationale: Value streams and ongoing operation belong to ITIL, not to the project method.

161.question_text: Which role authorises the budget dedicated to consuming a service?
161.explanation: The sponsor authorises the funding for consuming the service within the consumer organisation.

A.rationale: This role authorises the budget needed to consume the service.

B.rationale: The user directly uses the service but does not necessarily authorise its funding.

C.rationale: The customer defines requirements and is accountable for the consumption outcomes, without being necessarily the budget authority.

D.rationale: It authorises changes and not the budget for consuming a service.

162.question_text: How does a service provider mainly contribute to value creation for the consumer?
162.explanation: The provider brings specialised resources and helps reduce certain risks, while value remains co-created with the consumer.

A.text: By providing specialised resources and reducing certain risks
A.rationale: The provider's specialisation complements the consumer's resources and capabilities.

B.text: By taking over the consumer's responsibility for outcomes
B.rationale: The customer remains accountable for outcomes; responsibilities stay shared.

C.text: By defining the consumer's business requirements on its behalf
C.rationale: Defining requirements is the customer's role within the consumer organisation.

D.text: By transferring ownership of its resources to the consumer
D.rationale: This describes a transfer of goods, one form of interaction, not the provider's main contribution.

163.question_text: In which part of a practice guide are recommendations for the practice's successful automation mainly found?
163.explanation: Recommendations about tools, data, and automations mainly belong to the "information and technology" dimension.

A.rationale: This dimension addresses technologies and their use to support the practice.

B.rationale: This part deals mainly with roles, skills, structures, and human aspects.

C.rationale: This part examines external relationships and dependencies.

D.rationale: This part mostly describes the activities, controls, and flow of work.

164.scenario: A team runs scheduled backups, monitors systems, and captures technical events.
164.question_text: Which lifecycle activity is mainly illustrated?
164.explanation: The "operate" activity maintains the ongoing running of products, services, and systems, notably through monitoring and recurring tasks.

A.rationale: Backups and monitoring are routine operational activities.

B.rationale: Support focuses mainly on interruptions and assistance needs.

C.rationale: Deliver concerns normal interactions with users and provision of the service.

D.rationale: Transition moves changes into the environments where they will be used.

165.question_text: Which criterion is particularly relevant when an organisation evaluates a service provided by a third party in the "acquire" activity?
165.explanation: The organisation must examine the quality, fit, risks, and capacity of external resources or services to support the desired outcomes.

A.text: The quality and fit of the resources or services obtained
A.rationale: Acquisition must ensure that external resources meet needs.

B.text: The speed of restoring internal incidents
B.rationale: That measure mainly concerns operational support.

C.rationale: A prototype belongs more to exploration and design.

D.text: The volume of calls received by the service desk
D.rationale: That data does not directly determine the quality of the acquired resource.

166.question_text: Which statement best describes a good in the context of a service offering?
166.explanation: A good is a tangible or transferable resource whose ownership or responsibility can pass from the provider to the consumer. It differs from temporary access to a resource and from an action performed by the provider.

A.text: A resource whose ownership is transferred to the consumer
A.rationale: Ownership passing to the consumer distinguishes goods from access to resources and service actions.

B.text: An activity performed by the provider to meet a consumer need
B.rationale: This proposal describes a service action and not a good.

C.text: A right of use granted without transfer of ownership
C.rationale: This proposal matches access to resources.

D.text: A set of agreed metrics for measuring quality
D.rationale: This proposal describes a service level.

167.question_text: Which of the following best describes user experience?
167.explanation: User experience gathers the perceptions and reactions of a person resulting from the actual or anticipated use of a product or service. It can form before, during, and after the interaction.

A.text: A user's functional and emotional experience with a product or service
A.rationale: User experience covers perceptions and reactions related to actual or anticipated use.

B.text: A customer's experience across the whole relationship and its touchpoints
B.rationale: This describes customer experience (CX), which is broader than UX.

C.text: The product's conformity with its functional and technical specification
C.rationale: Conformity may influence experience, but does not define it.

D.text: The experience targets agreed with users in an experience level agreement
D.rationale: An XLA sets experience targets; it is an agreement, not the experience itself.

168.question_text: Which ITIL term denotes a person or group of persons with functions, responsibilities, authorities, and relationships of their own for achieving objectives?
168.explanation: An organization can be a complete entity or an identifiable part of a larger entity. It is defined by its functions, responsibilities, authorities, and relationships.

A.rationale: This definition matches the ITIL term "organization".

B.rationale: A practice is a set of organizational capabilities designed for performing work.

C.rationale: A value stream is a series of steps used to create and deliver value.

D.rationale: An offering describes the services, goods, and access proposed to a group of consumers.

169.question_text: Which statement about the service consumer role is correct?
169.explanation: The service consumer is a generic role that can include the customer, user, and sponsor roles. A person or group can hold several of these roles depending on the context.

A.text: It can encompass the customer, user, and sponsor roles
A.rationale: These three roles are possible specialisations of the service consumer.

B.text: It is a sub-role of the customer, alongside the user and the sponsor
B.rationale: This reverses the hierarchy: customer, user, and sponsor are sub-roles of the consumer.

C.text: It is the role that creates and improves digital products for the market
C.rationale: This describes the digital product vendor.

D.text: It is held by the organisation that manages the resources to provide the service
D.rationale: This describes the service provider role.

173.scenario: An outsourced payroll service removes the operating cost of an old server but adds subscription and migration fees.
173.question_text: Which cost analysis best fits ITIL?
173.explanation: A service can remove some costs from the consumer while imposing others. Evaluating value must consider both categories rather than only the sticker price.

A.text: Compare the costs the service removes with those it imposes
A.rationale: ITIL distinguishes costs removed and costs introduced by service consumption.

B.text: Assess the subscription price against the providers' market rates
B.rationale: Benchmarking the price ignores the costs removed and the other costs imposed on the consumer.

C.text: Treat the costs moved to the provider as no longer relevant to the consumer
C.rationale: The consumer may still bear those costs indirectly through the price or other resources.

D.text: Base the decision on the provider's internal cost of delivering the service
D.rationale: The consumer's value perception depends on its own costs and outcomes.

174.scenario: A cloud solution reduces the risk of a local hardware failure but introduces dependency on the internet connection and on the provider.
174.question_text: Which conclusion is the most appropriate?
174.explanation: Consuming a service can reduce some risks and introduce new ones. The decision must evaluate the whole risk profile rather than assume a service eliminates all uncertainty.

A.text: The service removes some risks while potentially imposing others
A.rationale: This answer reflects the two possible effects of a service on the consumer's risks.

B.text: The service reduces risk, so a new risk assessment is unnecessary
B.rationale: The scenario specifically shows new dependencies that need assessing.

C.text: The new dependencies are the provider's responsibility, not the consumer's
C.rationale: Responsibilities and risks remain shared based on the relationship and agreements.

D.text: Risk should be assessed when the first connection outage occurs
D.rationale: Risk must be considered before and during service consumption.

175.question_text: Which elements mainly contribute to determining whether a service is fit for use?
175.explanation: Warranty concerns the assurance that a service will meet agreed conditions of use. It is generally associated with availability, capacity, continuity, and security.

A.rationale: These conditions are the main aspects used to assess warranty.

B.rationale: Features mainly belong to utility, while the other terms are not the four warranty conditions.

C.rationale: These elements belong to the four management dimensions.

D.rationale: These are lifecycle activities, not warranty conditions.

176.question_text: Which proposition best represents the aspects that together influence a service's quality?
176.explanation: Service quality is broader than a single technical measure. It can be assessed through the service's utility, warranty, experience, and sustainability.

A.rationale: These aspects together contribute to the service's ability to meet needs.

B.rationale: These are aspects of warranty, just one of the four value characteristics.

C.rationale: This is the ITIL 4 view; Version 5 adds user experience and sustainability.

D.text: The number of releases and changes performed
D.rationale: The volume of modifications does not demonstrate the quality achieved.

177.scenario: A provider gradually replaces its technicians' manual interventions with self-service and controlled automations.
177.question_text: Why can this shift be advantageous for a digital service?
177.explanation: Reducing manual actions can increase scalability, speed, and consistency, provided the necessary controls and assistance remain in place. The goal is not to eliminate every useful interaction.

A.text: It increases the scalability, speed, and consistency of service execution
A.rationale: Automation and self-service reduce dependency on repetitive manual interventions.

B.text: It removes the need for a service desk as the single point of contact
B.rationale: Self-service complements the service desk; some situations still require human intervention.

C.text: It turns access to resources into a transfer of goods for the consumer
C.rationale: The execution mode does not change the nature of the offering component.

D.text: It transfers responsibility for service quality to the consumer
D.rationale: The provider remains accountable for the agreed commitments and quality.

178.scenario: A software vendor develops an application sold to an integrator. The integrator then uses it to deliver a managed service to its own customers.
178.question_text: Which statement best describes the vendor's role?
178.explanation: The digital product provider creates and improves the product but does not necessarily deliver the final service to users. Several organisations can therefore contribute to a single offering.

A.text: It creates the digital product, while the integrator provides the service
A.rationale: Product development and service delivery belong here to different organisations.

B.text: It is the sponsor of the managed service for the end customers
B.rationale: The sponsor belongs to the consumer organisation and authorises the budget.

C.text: It is the service provider that delivers the managed service to end customers
C.rationale: The integrator, not the vendor, provides the managed service.

D.text: It is the user of the managed service delivered by the integrator
D.rationale: Producing the application does not make the vendor a consumer of the final service.

179.scenario: An initially standardised relationship evolves after several years towards a shared roadmap, joint investments, and shared risks.
179.question_text: Which statement is the most correct?
179.explanation: The service relationship type is not necessarily permanent. It can evolve as trust, interdependence, and the parties' strategic objectives change.

A.text: The relationship can evolve from a basic relationship into a collaborative one
A.rationale: Joint investments and shared risks indicate a shift towards strategic collaboration.

B.text: A basic relationship stays basic because it was set up as standardised
B.rationale: Relationships can evolve depending on needs and the partnership's maturity.

C.text: The relationship has evolved into a cooperative relationship
C.rationale: A cooperative relationship involves more coordination, but not shared strategic objectives, investments, or risks.

D.text: The relationship stops being a service relationship as soon as risks are shared
D.rationale: Shared risks are on the contrary characteristic of a more collaborative relationship.

180.question_text: Which statement best distinguishes a service level from overall service quality?
180.explanation: A service level translates certain aspects of quality into defined metrics. Overall quality remains broader and also includes characteristics or perceptions not fully captured by those metrics.

A.text: A service level measures agreed aspects of quality; overall quality is broader
A.rationale: Service level metrics do not necessarily cover the whole experience and set of needs.

B.text: Service quality is the documented agreement on the expected service levels
B.rationale: This describes an SLA, not service quality.

C.text: A service level is the totality of characteristics that satisfy stated needs
C.rationale: This is the definition of service quality, not of a service level.

D.text: Service quality is measured by the SLA, while a service level reflects perception
D.rationale: This inverts the concepts: service levels are metrics and perception belongs to overall quality.

181.scenario: A transformation creates new roles, but decision-making authorities remain unclear and teams use incompatible communication channels.
181.question_text: Which aspect of the "organizations and people" dimension must be tackled as a priority?
181.explanation: This dimension includes structures, authority systems, responsibilities, culture, and communication. Defining job titles alone is not enough to enable effective collaboration.

A.text: Clarify roles, decision authorities, and communication channels
A.rationale: The difficulties described directly concern the organisation of work and decisions.

B.text: Deploy a common collaboration tool before clarifying roles
B.rationale: A tool belongs to the information and technology dimension and does not resolve ambiguous authority.

C.text: Review supplier contracts to align them with the new roles
C.rationale: This belongs to the partners and suppliers dimension; the problem described is internal.

D.text: Redesign the workflows and handoffs between the teams' activities
D.rationale: This belongs to the value streams and processes dimension; the problem is authority and communication.

182.scenario: A team selects a very high-performance platform, but it is incompatible with the existing architecture, the available skills, and the data protection requirements.
182.question_text: Which approach best fits the "information and technology" dimension?
182.explanation: The technology choice must take into account architecture, information, skills, security, and regulatory constraints. A product's isolated performance is not enough.

A.text: Assess fit with the architecture, skills, and security and compliance needs
A.rationale: The dimension requires analysis of the whole information and technology ecosystem.

B.text: Select the platform on its benchmark performance, then adapt the architecture
B.rationale: High performance does not compensate for the incompatibilities and risks described.

C.text: Ask the supplier to handle data protection requirements after purchase
C.rationale: Constraints must be analysed before the decision and cannot simply be transferred.

D.text: Let the platform's features define the team's processes and roles
D.rationale: Processes and technologies must be designed coherently, without the tool dictating them.

183.scenario: An organisation hesitates between developing a capability in-house and entrusting it to a specialised supplier.
183.question_text: Which set of factors should mainly guide its sourcing strategy?
183.explanation: The sourcing decision depends notably on strategic direction, costs, resource availability, required expertise, culture, external constraints, and demand variations.

A.text: Strategy, available expertise, costs, culture, constraints, and demand
A.rationale: These factors enable a balanced evaluation of using partners.

B.text: The unit price proposed by the supplier and its contractual payment terms
B.rationale: Price covers neither risks, expertise, nor strategic alignment.

C.text: The number of suppliers in the market and their market share
C.rationale: Market conditions are one factor, but they are not enough to determine the strategy.

D.text: The technical manager's preference and the team's current workload
D.rationale: The decision must be based on the organisational context and the service's needs.

184.question_text: Which statement correctly distinguishes a process from a value stream?
184.explanation: A process transforms inputs into outputs through linked activities. A value stream combines steps, which may mobilise several processes and practices, to create and deliver value to a stakeholder.

A.text: A process turns inputs into outputs; a value stream creates and delivers value
A.rationale: This distinction separates the operational mechanism from the end-to-end value perspective.

B.text: A process spans organisations; a value stream stays within one team
B.rationale: Both can cross organisational boundaries.

C.text: A value stream is just one activity within a process that transforms inputs into outputs
C.rationale: This reverses the relationship: a value stream can combine several processes and practices.

D.text: A process delivers value to external customers; a value stream supports it internally
D.rationale: This confuses core and enabling streams; a process is not defined by direct external value.

185.scenario: A government announces a national priority favouring digital sovereignty, without a new legal obligation yet in force.
185.question_text: Which PESTLE factor is mainly illustrated?
185.explanation: A governmental orientation or priority mainly belongs to the political factor. It differs from the legal factor, which concerns laws, regulations, and legally binding obligations.

A.rationale: The scenario describes a governmental orientation rather than a rule already binding.

B.rationale: No law or legally binding obligation is yet in force.

C.rationale: Digital sovereignty concerns technology, but the described trigger is a political decision.

D.rationale: The scenario does not mainly focus on societal behaviours or expectations.

186.scenario: A team receives a specific request to build an application, but interviews reveal that the business problem could be solved without a new piece of software.
186.question_text: Which action best matches the "discover" activity?
186.explanation: Discover seeks to understand context, needs, opportunities, risks, and assumptions before choosing a solution. This prevents mistaking a solution request for the real need.

A.text: Validate the business problem and desired outcomes before choosing a solution
A.rationale: This action reduces uncertainty and matches the purpose of discovery.

B.text: Start building the requested application in short iterations with user feedback
B.rationale: Iterating on the build still commits to a solution before the real need is validated.

C.text: Write the detailed specification of the requested application
C.rationale: This belongs to design and assumes the application is the right answer.

D.text: Acquire the licences and resources needed for the new software
D.rationale: This belongs to the acquire activity and commits resources before the need is confirmed.

187.scenario: A design team focuses only on the visible features and ignores the support model, the suppliers, the data, and the skills required.
187.question_text: Which correction best fits the "design" activity?
187.explanation: Design must consider the product or service as a whole, across the four dimensions and the lifecycle. A functional interface is not enough if operation, support, and the required capabilities are not designed.

A.text: Extend the design to the four dimensions and to operational and support needs
A.rationale: Holistic design prepares a viable solution across its whole lifecycle.

B.text: Defer support and supplier decisions to the transition activity
B.rationale: Transition introduces the solution into use; support and supplier needs must be designed beforehand.

C.text: Refine the functional specification and test the interface prototypes with users
C.rationale: This deepens the visible features but still ignores support, suppliers, data, and skills.

D.text: Let suppliers define the support model once the product is built
D.rationale: Supplier dependencies and responsibilities must be explicitly designed and agreed.

188.scenario: A product has passed its technical tests, but users are not trained, data has not been migrated, and support has no procedure.
188.question_text: Which activity should mainly coordinate preparation before operational use?
188.explanation: Transition aims to smoothly introduce new or changed products and services into their usage environment. Preparation includes people, data, support, communications, and technical changes.

A.rationale: The gaps described directly concern the state of readiness for moving into operational use.

B.rationale: The technical solution is already implemented and tested; the problem is about introducing it into service.

C.rationale: Needs have already been turned into a product; it is no longer about understanding the initial opportunity.

D.rationale: Operation starts when the product is in ongoing running.

189.scenario: A team runs scheduled backups, monitors capacity, handles events, and keeps components in operational condition on a daily basis.
189.question_text: Why do these tasks mainly belong to the "operate" activity rather than to "support"?
189.explanation: Operate covers the running, monitoring, and routine upkeep of products and services. Support mainly steps in to resolve interruptions, difficulties, or assistance needs.

A.text: They routinely maintain the running and performance of systems
A.rationale: The planned, recurring nature of the tasks matches operation.

B.text: They restore the service after users report an interruption
B.rationale: The scenario describes routine tasks and not a response to an interruption.

C.text: They introduce a new or changed product into live use
C.rationale: That would rather belong to transition.

D.text: They provide users with access and handle their routine requests
D.rationale: This describes the deliver activity.

190.question_text: Which statement about the organisation of the eight lifecycle activities is correct?
190.explanation: Lifecycle activities are types of work that are interconnected, not mandatory departments. A single team can contribute to several activities and several activities can run in parallel.

A.text: They do not necessarily correspond to eight distinct teams or departments
A.rationale: ITIL describes activities that can be adapted to the organisation's operating model.

B.text: Each activity should be assigned to a dedicated department
B.rationale: The model does not prescribe a team or department structure.

C.text: Each person should be assigned to one specific activity
C.rationale: Responsibilities can span several activities depending on skills and the value stream.

D.text: The activities must be performed in order, from Discover to Support
D.rationale: The lifecycle is interconnected, iterative, and non-linear.

191.question_text: Which elements are respectively the main inputs and the output of the ITIL Value System?
191.explanation: The ITIL Value System transforms opportunity and demand into value through its components and activities. Value is not a guaranteed input: it is co-created by the system's operation.

A.text: Opportunity and demand are inputs; value is the output
A.rationale: This relationship describes the overall operation of the ITIL Value System.

B.text: Value and outcomes are inputs; practices are the output
B.rationale: Practices are enabling components, while value is the desired output.

C.text: Incidents are the inputs; changes are the output
C.rationale: These elements can appear in some flows but do not define the overall system.

D.text: Governance is the input; the SLA is the output
D.rationale: Governance is a component of the system, and an SLA is not its overall output.

192.scenario: An organisation applies the guiding principles separately from its governance, practices, and value chain.
192.question_text: Which risk does this approach mainly create?
192.explanation: The ITIL Value System's components are designed to work together. Isolating them can cause inconsistent decisions and prevent the effective transformation of opportunity and demand into value.

A.text: Fragmentation that stops the components working together to create value
A.rationale: The ITIL Value System depends on the interactions between its components.

B.text: Faster decisions, because each component can evolve independently of the others
B.rationale: Independence may seem faster but produces inconsistent decisions; the components must work together.

C.text: Practices being replaced by the eight lifecycle activities
C.rationale: Practices and activities remain distinct concepts even when they interact.

D.text: A shift of accountability from the governing body to the practices
D.rationale: Separating the principles does not change governance accountability.

193.question_text: Which statement about the use of the ITIL guiding principles is correct?
193.explanation: The guiding principles are universal recommendations that must be considered in every circumstance. Their application still has to be adapted to context and does not constitute a rigid procedure.

A.text: They are relevant in all situations, but their use is adapted to context
A.rationale: The principles guide decisions without imposing a single procedure.

B.text: Each principle is linked to one specific activity of the product and service lifecycle
B.rationale: The principles can apply across activities and decisions.

C.text: They should be applied one at a time in a defined order
C.rationale: The principles interact and have no order; several are generally considered together.

D.text: They are mandatory rules that replace the organisation's own policies
D.rationale: They orient decisions but do not replace policies or governance.

194.scenario: An improvement reduces internal processing time but forces customers to provide more information and increases their overall effort.
194.question_text: Which analysis best applies the "focus on value" principle?
194.explanation: Value must be considered from the perspective of consumers and other stakeholders, including experience and indirect effects. An internal optimisation can destroy value if it shifts the effort to the customer.

A.text: Assess the overall effect on customer outcomes and experience
A.rationale: The principle requires linking every activity to the value actually perceived.

B.text: Keep the improvement because internal time has decreased
B.rationale: The local gain may be cancelled out by the extra effort imposed on the customer.

C.text: Measure success by the number of internal steps removed
C.rationale: The simplicity of the internal process does not prove value creation.

D.text: Automate the new information requests to cut internal costs further
D.rationale: This pursues internal efficiency and ignores the extra effort imposed on customers.

195.scenario: Members of a team know their process so well that they no longer notice certain workarounds and unnecessary waits.
195.question_text: Which action is particularly useful under the "start where you are" principle?
195.explanation: A person unfamiliar with the service can observe without the preconceptions of teams used to the current way of working. This perspective complements the specialists' data and experience.

A.text: Ask someone unfamiliar with the service to observe the work
A.rationale: A fresh eye can reveal practices that have become invisible to people used to them.

B.text: Ask the most experienced team members to document the process
B.rationale: Experienced members often share the same blind spots.

C.text: Redesign the process from scratch using a reference model
C.rationale: The principle recommends assessing what exists before deciding what to change.

D.text: Base the assessment on the official process documentation
D.rationale: Documentation can differ from the work actually performed.

197.scenario: A manager invites every person in the company to every meeting to demonstrate maximum collaboration.
197.question_text: Which correction best fits the guiding principle?
197.explanation: Effective collaboration involves the right people, at the right time, and at the appropriate level. It means neither universal participation nor a mandatory pursuit of full consensus.

A.text: Involve the relevant stakeholders for each decision
A.rationale: Collaboration must be targeted to produce better decisions without overload.

B.text: Keep the wide invitations to maximise visibility across the company
B.rationale: Excessive participation can slow down work and reduce the quality of exchanges.

C.text: Delegate each decision to a single accountable manager
C.rationale: This approach risks excluding essential knowledge and perspectives.

D.text: Require full consensus of the attendees before acting
D.rationale: Collaboration does not require full consensus.

198.scenario: A team publishes all its raw data to the whole organisation, but decision-makers cannot identify the relevant information.
198.question_text: How should visibility be improved according to ITIL?
198.explanation: Visibility must give stakeholders the relevant, understandable, and timely information they need. Making everything visible without context can create noise rather than support decisions.

A.text: Share relevant information in a form suited to each audience
A.rationale: Useful visibility depends on the audience, need, and context.

B.text: Publish the raw data more often so it stays up to date
B.rationale: More frequent raw data does not help decision-makers find what matters.

C.text: Report problems to decision-makers once they are resolved
C.rationale: This approach prevents stakeholders from understanding risks and acting in time.

D.text: Replace the data with the teams' own assessments of their progress
D.rationale: Self-assessments without evidence reduce the reliability of the information.

199.scenario: An analysis reveals a weakness in a software component that could cause interruptions, but no complete diagnosis of the associated problem has yet been documented.
199.question_text: Which term best describes the identified weakness?
199.explanation: An error is a fault or vulnerability likely to cause incidents. A known error corresponds to a problem that has already been analysed but not yet resolved.

A.rationale: The technical weakness likely to cause incidents corresponds to an error.

B.rationale: This term assumes that a problem has already been analysed and remains unresolved.

C.rationale: No predefined user request is described.

D.rationale: A service level is a set of quality metrics.

200.scenario: A process has few steps, but each step requires several validations with no effect on risk or value.
200.question_text: Which conclusion best fits the "keep it simple and practical" principle?
200.explanation: Simplicity is not measured only by the number of steps. Every activity, control, or piece of information should have an identifiable contribution to value, risk, or a necessary outcome.

A.text: Examine and remove validations that contribute to no necessary outcome
A.rationale: The principle recommends the minimum elements required to achieve the objective.

B.text: Keep the validations because the process already has few steps
B.rationale: A step can remain useless or excessively complex even in a short process.

C.text: Add validations to make the process more complete
C.rationale: Additional complexity must be justified by a real contribution.

D.text: Automate the validations before evaluating their usefulness
D.rationale: Automating a useless activity preserves the waste.

201.scenario: An organisation automates the response to every request, including those requiring empathy, judgement, and handling of sensitive exceptions.
201.question_text: Which approach best fits the "optimize and automate" principle?
201.explanation: Automation should be used where it improves value, consistency, and efficiency. Human interventions should be kept when they bring judgement, creativity, or a relationship that automation does not adequately provide.

A.text: Automate repetitive tasks and keep human judgement where it adds value
A.rationale: Automation should support optimised work rather than indiscriminately remove people.

B.text: Automate each activity once it becomes technically feasible
B.rationale: Technical feasibility does not prove that automation improves value or reduces risk.

C.text: Pause automation until each exception has a documented manual procedure
C.rationale: Designing for each exception adds complexity; automate where it adds value.

D.text: Measure the automation's success by the reduction in headcount
D.rationale: The principle aims at optimising value and outcomes, not a staffing objective.

202.scenario: The governing body analyses current performance, stakeholder needs, and changes in the external environment.
202.question_text: Which governance activity does this mainly correspond to?
202.explanation: Evaluate consists of examining the organisation, its environment, its options, and stakeholder needs. This activity provides the understanding needed before setting direction.

A.rationale: Analysing the context, performance, and needs corresponds to evaluation.

B.rationale: Direct consists of setting orientation, priorities, and policies.

C.rationale: Monitor mainly checks execution and compliance with the direction given.

D.rationale: Build is a lifecycle activity, not a governance activity.

203.scenario: After reviewing several options, the board sets investment priorities, approves a risk policy, and communicates the direction to management.
203.question_text: Which governance activity does this mainly correspond to?
203.explanation: Direct consists of assigning the orientation, policies, and priorities that guide the organisation's management. This activity generally follows the evaluation of context and options.

A.rationale: Setting priorities and policies corresponds to the direct activity.

B.rationale: Evaluation analyses the options; the scenario describes the decision and direction chosen.

C.rationale: Monitoring checks results and compliance after execution.

D.rationale: Discover concerns product or service needs and opportunities, not the governance direction.

204.scenario: A board delegates the decision on certain digital investments to a committee.
204.question_text: Which statement about governance responsibility is the most correct?
204.explanation: Decision-making authority can be delegated, but the governing body remains accountable for how that authority is exercised and for the outcomes of governance.

A.text: Authority can be delegated, but the ultimate governance accountability remains
A.rationale: Delegation does not remove the obligation of oversight and accountability.

B.text: Delegation transfers ultimate accountability to the committee
B.rationale: The governing body keeps the ultimate accountability for governance.

C.text: Governance decisions must be taken by the board itself
C.rationale: Framed delegation is possible when it is clearly defined and supervised.

D.text: The committee becomes responsible for day-to-day management
D.rationale: Delegated governance authority is not day-to-day management.

205.scenario: An innovation stream uses the "design" activity twice and runs some "acquire" and "build" tasks in parallel.
205.question_text: Why can this use be correct?
205.explanation: Value chain activities can be used several times, in different orders, and sometimes in parallel within a value stream. The model does not impose a single sequence.

A.text: Value chain activities can be combined and repeated to suit the value stream
A.rationale: The value chain is flexible and adapts to the work needed to create value.

B.text: Each activity should appear once per value stream to avoid rework
B.rationale: A stream can return to an activity when new information or decisions are needed.

C.text: The activities must follow the order from Discover to Support
C.rationale: ITIL does not prescribe a universal sequence.

D.text: It is correct because Acquire and Build form one combined value chain activity
D.rationale: In Version 5, Acquire and Build are separate activities; "obtain/build" was an ITIL 4 activity.

206.question_text: What lets an organisation consistently execute its digital product and service management activities?
